Subject: . FTC and TIOJ Tar and Nicotine Relationships
The FTC and TIoJ tar and nicotine data supplied by J.M. Garman on November 11,
1g89 and January 8, 1990 have been analyzed to: define the relationships:
between measurements: from the two methods.
There were forty FTC/TIOJ pairs of tar and nicotine averages for 27 brands.
Thirteen of the brands ware measured twice each from two different week-ending
samples. Eight of the brands measured from only one week-ending sample were
measured at a different time and on a dlfferent machine from all of the other
brands.
The statistical analyses were based only on average tar and nicotine values
and on butt-length differences. Ftc butt lengths were 0, 2, 3, or 5mm: shorter
than TIoJ butt lengths. The primary differences between the two methods,
which would cause different results, are butt length and air flow. The FTC
method (as applied by Philip Morris) has greater air flow through the smoking
machine and so would be expected to give lower deliveries because of faster
burning between puffs. Where the two methods differ in butt length, the
method with the: shorter butt length (more rod available for smoking) would be
expected to give higher values due to that effect.
A reasonable way to summarize the relationship between FTC and TIOJ values is
to relate the difference (TIOJ minus FTC) to the magnitude of the values
(represented by the average of. FTC: and TIOJ). Intuitively, then, that
difference should be proportional to the magnitude of the values, and the
effect of a butt-length difference should be proportional. to both the butt-
length difference and, again, to the magnitude of: values. Hathematically,
